paper_b.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (Kingma & Ba, 2014)

metadata.description: AdamW is a bug-fix improvement (BI) of Adam. The core Adam algorithm (adaptive moment estimation with bias correction) is preserved entirely; AdamW fixes a subtle but impactful bug: standard Adam applies L2 regularization inside the gradient, so the regularization gets scaled by the adaptive learning rate (1/sqrt(v_hat)), coupling weight decay with gradient history. AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive update, applying it as a separate multiplicative step on the weights. Same optimizer core, corrected regularization.

matches.explanation: AdamW preserves Adam's first and second moment estimates (m_t, v_t) with the same exponential moving average formulas and decay rates (beta_1, beta_2). No change.
AdamW preserves Adam's bias correction (m_hat_t = m_t/(1-beta_1^t), v_hat_t = v_t/(1-beta_2^t)). No change.

THE key difference. Adam: $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \alpha \hat{m}_t / (\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon)$ where the gradient $g_t$ may include the L2 term $\lambda\theta$. AdamW: $\theta_t = (1-\lambda)\theta_{t-1} - \alpha \hat{m}_t / (\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon)$ where $g_t = \nabla f_t$ (no L2 term in gradient) and weight decay is applied separately. The adaptive update $\alpha \hat{m}_t/(\sqrt{\hat{v}_t}+\epsilon)$ is identical; the regularization mechanism differs.

Both describe the same problematic interaction: in Adam with L2 regularization, the regularization gradient $\lambda\theta$ is scaled by $1/\sqrt{\hat{v}_t}$, making effective weight decay dependent on the adaptive learning rate. Adam acknowledges L2 regularization implicitly; AdamW identifies this coupling as the core problem to fix.
The analysis of hyperparameter coupling (optimal weight decay depends on learning rate in Adam but not in AdamW) is a contribution specific to the AdamW paper.
SGDW (decoupled weight decay for SGD, shown to be equivalent to L2 for SGD) is a completeness result in the AdamW paper. Not relevant to Adam.

Both present empirical results on deep learning tasks. Adam shows convergence speed advantages over SGD/AdaGrad/RMSProp. AdamW shows generalization advantages over Adam+L2, partially closing the Adam-vs-SGD gap. Different claims: Adam focuses on optimization speed; AdamW focuses on generalization quality.
AdamW with warm restarts (AdamWR) is a contribution specific to the AdamW paper, combining the fix with cosine annealing schedules.
Adam's convergence analysis (O(sqrt(T)) regret for online convex optimization) is a theoretical contribution not present in AdamW. AdamW does not provide a revised convergence analysis.

unmatched_paper_a_explanations.DP_AW.3: SGDW definition for completeness. Specific to AdamW paper.
unmatched_paper_a_explanations.DP_AW.4: Hyperparameter coupling analysis. Unique contribution of AdamW.
unmatched_paper_a_explanations.TP_AW.2: AdamW with warm restarts. Combination specific to AdamW paper.

unmatched_paper_b_explanations.TP_ADAM.1: Adam convergence theorem (O(sqrt(T)) regret). Theoretical analysis not revised in AdamW.

summary: AdamW is a targeted bug-fix improvement (BI) of Adam. The entire Adam algorithm (exponential moving averages of gradient and squared gradient, bias correction, per-parameter adaptive learning rates) is preserved unchanged. The single modification: L2 regularization is removed from the gradient input to Adam and instead applied as a separate multiplicative weight decay step on the parameters. This fixes the unintended coupling between regularization strength and adaptive learning rates, where in standard Adam+L2, parameters with large gradient history receive weaker regularization. The fix is one line of code but has significant practical impact: better generalization, simplified hyperparameter tuning (learning rate and weight decay decouple), and partial closing of the Adam-vs-SGD generalization gap on vision tasks.
